claim: The organization of micron-sized, multi-microtubule arrays from individual microtubules is essential for diverse cellular functions.
source: The organization of micron-sized, multi-microtubule arrays from individual microtubules is essential for diverse cellular functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about microtubule function presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this sentence, but draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Micron-scale geometrical features of individual microtubules and polymer networks, such as microtubule length, overlap length, contact angle, and lattice defects, can regulate the activity of microtubule-associated proteins and modulate polymer dynamics.
source: Recent studies reveal that micron-scale geometrical features of individual microtubules and polymer networks, such as microtubule length, overlap length, contact angle, and lattice defects, can also regulate the activity of microtubule-associated proteins and modulate polymer dynamics.
evidence: The claim references 'recent studies' indicating citation-based support for this assertion.

claim: The orientation of coaligned, overlapping microtubules in the cortex of plant cells specifies the axis of cell elongation.
source: For instance, the orientation of coaligned, overlapping microtubules in the cortex of plant cells specifies the axis of cell elongation, and the polarity of long microtubule bundles in neurons distinguishes axons from dendrites (Chen et al., 2016; Kelliher et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Kelliher et al., 2019.

claim: The polarity of long microtubule bundles in neurons distinguishes axons from dendrites.
source: For instance, the orientation of coaligned, overlapping microtubules in the cortex of plant cells specifies the axis of cell elongation, and the polarity of long microtubule bundles in neurons distinguishes axons from dendrites (Chen et al., 2016; Kelliher et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Kelliher et al., 2019.

claim: Microtubules are characterized by their inherent dynamic instability and cycle between phases of polymerization and depolymerization.
source: Microtubules are characterized by their inherent dynamic instability and cycle between phases of polymerization and depolymerization (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984, a foundational study on microtubule dynamics.

claim: Polymerization dynamics of individual microtubule filaments are sensitive to the concentration of soluble tubulin heterodimers.
source: First, polymerization dynamics of individual microtubule filaments are sensitive to the concentration of soluble tubulin heterodimers which constitute their building blocks (Walker et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Walker et al., 1988.

claim: Tubulin levels are autoregulated through translational control by tubulin itself.
source: In cells, tubulin levels are in turn autoregulated through translational control by tubulin itself (Cleveland, 1988; Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cleveland, 1988 and Lin et al., 2020.

claim: Chemical modifications of tubulin at the amino acid level can affect the inherent physical properties of the polymer and also regulate MAP activity.
source: These chemical modifications of tubulin at the amino acid level can affect the inherent physical properties of the polymer and also regulate MAP activity (Alper et al., 2014; Kaul et al., 2014; Sirajuddin et al., 2014; Leo et al., 2015; Valenstein and Roll-Mecak, 2016; Bailey et al., 2015; Schwarz et al., 1998; Robison et al., 2016; Portran et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on tubulin modifications.

claim: Branching microtubule nucleation has been observed to generate new microtubules at distinct orientation to the parent tubule in diverse cell types.
source: Since its first report in the alga Nitella tasmanica, branching nucleation has been observed to generate new microtubules at distinct orientation to the parent tubule in diverse cell types (O. WASTENEYS and E. WILLIAMSON, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to O. WASTENEYS and E. WILLIAMSON, 1989.

claim: Newly nucleated microtubules are parallel to the parent in the spindle and neuronal axons.
source: For example, newly nucleated microtubules are parallel to the parent in the spindle and neuronal axons, anti-parallel in arrays in yeast interphase cells and Arabidopsis pavement cells, and oriented at an angle of 40° with respect to the parent microtubule in plant cortical arrays (Janson et al., 2005; Murata et al., 2005; Petry et al., 2013; Sánchez-Huertas et al., 2016; Yagi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on branching nucleation.

claim: Newly nucleated microtubules are anti-parallel in arrays in yeast interphase cells and Arabidopsis pavement cells.
source: For example, newly nucleated microtubules are parallel to the parent in the spindle and neuronal axons, anti-parallel in arrays in yeast interphase cells and Arabidopsis pavement cells, and oriented at an angle of 40° with respect to the parent microtubule in plant cortical arrays (Janson et al., 2005; Murata et al., 2005; Petry et al., 2013; Sánchez-Huertas et al., 2016; Yagi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on branching nucleation.

claim: Newly nucleated microtubules are oriented at an angle of 40° with respect to the parent microtubule in plant cortical arrays.
source: For example, newly nucleated microtubules are parallel to the parent in the spindle and neuronal axons, anti-parallel in arrays in yeast interphase cells and Arabidopsis pavement cells, and oriented at an angle of 40° with respect to the parent microtubule in plant cortical arrays (Janson et al., 2005; Murata et al., 2005; Petry et al., 2013; Sánchez-Huertas et al., 2016; Yagi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on branching nucleation.

claim: γ-TuRC is a cone-shaped protein assembly, over 2 MDa in size.
source: γ-TuRC is a cone-shaped protein assembly, over 2 MDa in size (Zheng et al., 1995; Oegema et al., 1999; Murphy et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to structural studies of γ-TuRC.

claim: γ-TuRC contains a ring of γ-tubulins, which serves as an initiation point for the assembly of α-β tubulin subunits into a cylindrical microtubule.
source: It contains a ring of γ-tubulins, which serves as an initiation point for the assembly of α-β tubulin subunits into a cylindrical microtubule (Kollman et al., 2008; Consolati et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Wieczorek et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on γ-TuRC structure and function.

claim: γ-TuRC must first be recruited to pre-existing microtubules through interaction with lattice-bound MAPs such as augmin and TPX2 to initiate branching nucleation.
source: To initiate branching nucleation, γ-TuRC must first be recruited to pre-existing microtubules through interaction with lattice-bound MAPs such as augmin and targeting protein for Xklp2 (TPX2) (Goshima et al., 2008; Petry et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2014; King and Petry, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on γ-TuRC recruitment.

claim: Neither augmin nor TPX2 enhances the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC in solution, but do so when bound to a microtubule lattice.
source: Notably, neither augmin nor TPX2 enhances the nucleation activity of γ-TuRC in solution, but do so when bound to a microtubule lattice, thus providing a route to microtubule nucleation on a pre-existing microtubule platform (Nakamura et al., 2010; Alfaro-Aco et al., 2020; Consolati et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on augmin and TPX2 function.

claim: Structural models for the ternary complex of augmin and γ-TuRC bound to the microtubule lattice predict that the stereospecificity of the bound γ-TuRC complex can restrict the angle and polarity of the newly nucleated microtubule with respect to the parent.
source: Structural models for the ternary complex of augmin and γ-TuRC bound to the microtubule lattice predict that the stereospecificity of the bound γ-TuRC complex can restrict the angle and polarity of the newly nucleated microtubule with respect to the parent, thereby specifying array architecture (Wieczorek et al., 2020; Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural modeling studies.

claim: Knock-outs and mutations of γ-TuRC subunits affect the distribution of microtubule branching angles in plant cells.
source: In support of the structural models, knock-outs and mutations of γ-TuRC subunits were seen to affect the distribution of microtubule branching angles in plant cells (Kong et al., 2010; Nakamura and Hashimoto, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies in plant cells.

claim: The nucleation sites for new microtubules are distributed all along the parent lattice, with no spatial bias toward either end.
source: Multiple in vitro studies show that the nucleation sites for new microtubules are distributed all along the parent lattice, with no spatial bias toward either end (Song et al., 2018; Alfaro-Aco et al., 2020; Tariq et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to in vitro studies.

claim: The length of the parent microtubule could modulate microtubule number in an array, with more branching sites on longer microtubules.
source: This suggests that the length of the parent microtubule could modulate microtubule number in an array, with more branching sites on longer microtubules.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that nucleation sites are distributed along the lattice.

claim: SSNA1 is observed to induce branching by splitting the microtubule lattice, in vitro.
source: Interestingly, in addition to promoting branching nucleation in a similar manner to γ-TuRC, SSNA1 is observed to induce branching by splitting the microtubule lattice, in vitro.
evidence: This claim describes an observation from in vitro experiments, implicitly referencing the Basnet et al., 2018 study mentioned in the next sentence.

claim: Subsequent tubulin polymerization on the splayed protofilaments can complete the cylindrical tubules to form a branched microtubule array.
source: Subsequent tubulin polymerization on the splayed protofilaments can complete the cylindrical tubules to form a branched microtubule array (Basnet et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Basnet et al., 2018.

claim: In vitro work suggests that tubulin-tubulin interactions on the lattice of the parent microtubule can direct the assembly of the partial tubules that make up doublets and triplets.
source: In vitro work suggests that tubulin-tubulin interactions on the lattice of the parent microtubule can direct the assembly of the partial tubules that make up doublets and triplets (Serrano et al., 1984; Schmidt-Cernohorska et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: Radial outgrowth from an MTOC leads to a reduction in microtubule density with increasing distance from the MTOC.
source: First, it is predicted that radial outgrowth from an MTOC leads to a reduction in microtubule density with increasing distance from the MTOC (Mitchison et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a predictive/modeling study.

claim: Branching nucleation on initial radial microtubules helps maintain microtubule density at sites that are distant from the MTOC.
source: Branching nucleation on these initial radial microtubules helps maintain microtubule density at sites that are distant from the MTOC (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and is an inference from the mechanism of branching nucleation.

claim: The kinetics of nucleation and the directional bias imparted to microtubules nucleated by branching nucleation is suited for relatively rapid assembly of parallel bundles of high density, as seen in kinetochore fibers during cell division.
source: Moreover, the kinetics of nucleation and the directional bias imparted to microtubules nucleated by this mechanism is suited for relatively rapid assembly of parallel bundles of high density, as seen in kinetochore fibers during cell division (David et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to David et al., 2019.

claim: Branching nucleation accounts for over 90% of microtubules found in Arabidopsis cortical arrays.
source: In fact, it accounts for over 90% of microtubules found in Arabidopsis cortical arrays and is also important in post-mitotic neurons after the centrosome is inactivated (Cunha-Ferreira et al., 2018; Nakamura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in Arabidopsis and neurons.

claim: Branching nucleation is important in post-mitotic neurons after the centrosome is inactivated.
source: In fact, it accounts for over 90% of microtubules found in Arabidopsis cortical arrays and is also important in post-mitotic neurons after the centrosome is inactivated (Cunha-Ferreira et al., 2018; Nakamura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in Arabidopsis and neurons.

claim: Microtubules that intersect at shallow contact angles (<40°) are selectively cross-linked by MAPs such as members of the MAP65 family to form coaligned bundles.
source: Microtubules that intersect at shallow contact angles (<40°) are selectively cross-linked by MAPs such as members of the MAP65 family to form coaligned bundles.
evidence: This claim is based on the work of Dixit and Cyr, 2004 mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: A steep contact angle (>40°) between a growing end and a pre-existing microtubule lattice generates a pushing force on the growing tip.
source: In contrast, a steep contact angle (>40°) between a growing end and a pre-existing microtubule lattice generates a pushing force on the growing tip (Chi and Ambrose, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chi and Ambrose, 2016.

claim: Pushing forces can induce catastrophes, likely through a reduction in the rate of tubulin addition at plus-ends.
source: Such forces can induce catastrophes, likely through a reduction in the rate of tubulin addition at plus-ends (Janson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Janson et al., 2003.

claim: The interaction between the motor kinesin-2 and the plus-tip tracking proteins APC and EB1 promote the parallel alignment of a growing microtubule with a pre-existing bundle following the point of encounter.
source: For example, in branched neurons, the interaction between the motor kinesin-2 and the plus-tip tracking proteins adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) and end-binding protein 1 (EB1) promote the parallel alignment of a growing microtubule with a pre-existing bundle following the point of encounter (Mattie et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mattie et al., 2010.

claim: The probability of coalignment depends on the microtubule-binding affinities and tip occupancy of the MAPs.
source: Reconstitution of tip guidance starting from randomly oriented dynamic microtubules and chimeric kinesins modified to bind to the plus-tip tracking EB1 have revealed that the probability of coalignment depends on the microtubule-binding affinities and tip occupancy of the MAPs (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: Tip guidance is found to be more probable at very low angles and close to 90°, but less so at intermediate (40°−85°) and high obtuse angles.
source: Tip guidance is found to be more probable at very low angles and close to 90°, but less so at intermediate (40°−85°) and high obtuse angles (Doodhi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doodhi et al., 2014.

claim: The rate of tubulin disassembly by the kinesin-5 motor Cin8p increases with microtubule length in budding yeast astral and kinetochore microtubules.
source: For example, in budding yeast astral and kinetochore microtubules, the rate of tubulin disassembly by the kinesin-5 motor Cin8p increases with microtubule length (Gardner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gardner et al., 2008.

claim: In vitro studies reveal that the rate of microtubule depolymerization by kinesin-8 family members Kip3p and Kif18A is proportional to microtubule length.
source: Similarly in vitro studies reveal that the rate of microtubule depolymerization by kinesin-8 family members Kip3p and Kif18A and the rate of microtubule polymerization by the budding yeast kinesin Kip2p are proportional to microtubule length (Figure 3(i); Gupta et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2006; Mayr et al., 2007; Varga et al., 2009; Hibbel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to in vitro studies and reference to Figure 3(i).

claim: The rate of microtubule polymerization by the budding yeast kinesin Kip2p is proportional to microtubule length.
source: Similarly in vitro studies reveal that the rate of microtubule depolymerization by kinesin-8 family members Kip3p and Kif18A and the rate of microtubule polymerization by the budding yeast kinesin Kip2p are proportional to microtubule length (Figure 3(i); Gupta et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2006; Mayr et al., 2007; Varga et al., 2009; Hibbel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to in vitro studies and reference to Figure 3(i).

claim: For highly processive motors with a slow dissociation rate from the microtubule end, such as Kip3p, the number of motors accumulated on the plus-ends is proportional to microtubule length.
source: For highly processive motors with a slow dissociation rate from the microtubule end, such as in the case of Kip3p, the number of motors accumulated on the plus-ends is proportional to microtubule length (Figure 3(i)).
evidence: This claim is based on the antenna model and is supported by reference to Figure 3(i).

claim: The budding yeast Cin8p motor switches from minus-end directed on single microtubules to a plus-end directed motor on anti-parallel overlaps.
source: Among kinesin-5 proteins, the budding yeast Cin8p motor switches from minus-end directed on single microtubules to a plus-end directed motor on anti-parallel overlaps (Kapitein et al., 2008; Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2011Roostalu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on Cin8p directionality.

claim: When a lattice-bound Cik1-Kar3 motor is coupled to a second dynamic microtubule via interaction with an EB1 homolog, the motor switches to plus-end directed movement.
source: When a lattice-bound Cik1-Kar3 motor is coupled to a second dynamic microtubule via interaction with an EB1 homolog, the motor switches to plus-end directed movement.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from Molodtsov et al., 2016 mentioned in the next sentence.

claim: Direct force measurements on pairs of microtubules cross-linked by Xenopus laevis kinesin-5 motors have revealed that sliding forces produced by the motor depend on the relative polarities of the microtubules they cross-link.
source: Direct force measurements on pairs of microtubules cross-linked by Xenopus laevis kinesin-5 motors have revealed that sliding forces produced by the motor depend on the relative polarities of the microtubules they cross-link (Shimamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shimamoto et al., 2015.

claim: On overlaps formed by anti-parallel microtubules, sliding forces were found to scale linearly with motor number.
source: On overlaps formed by anti-parallel microtubules, sliding forces were found to scale linearly with motor number whereas on parallel overlaps they were bidirectional, smaller in magnitude, and independent of motor number (Figure 3(ii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3(ii) and is based on data from Shimamoto et al., 2015.

claim: On parallel overlaps, sliding forces were bidirectional, smaller in magnitude, and independent of motor number.
source: On overlaps formed by anti-parallel microtubules, sliding forces were found to scale linearly with motor number whereas on parallel overlaps they were bidirectional, smaller in magnitude, and independent of motor number (Figure 3(ii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3(ii) and is based on data from Shimamoto et al., 2015.

claim: Ase1p resists motor forces by producing a braking force that increases as motor-mediated sliding progresses.
source: In vitro studies have shown that Ase1p resists motor forces by producing a braking force that increases as motor-mediated sliding progresses (Figure 3(ii); Janson et al., 2007; Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies and reference to Figure 3(ii).

claim: When Ase1p cross-linked microtubules are moved apart by motors, the overlap shrinks, resulting in an increase in Ase1p density, due to its low off-rate from overlaps.
source: When Ase1p cross-linked microtubules are moved apart by motors, the overlap shrinks, resulting in an increase in Ase1p density, due to its low off-rate from overlaps (Figure 3(ii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3(ii) and is based on the mechanism described in the text.

claim: The rate of spindle elongation which is driven by the kinesin-mediated sliding of anti-parallel microtubules, is higher when the overlaps between microtubules are longer in fission yeast.
source: In fission yeast, the rate of spindle elongation which is driven by the kinesin-mediated sliding of anti-parallel microtubules, is higher when the overlaps between microtubules are longer (Krüger et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krüger et al., 2019.

claim: In multi-motor surface gliding assays with conventional kinesin, microtubule movement velocity is independent of microtubule length.
source: For example, in multi-motor surface gliding assays with conventional kinesin, microtubule movement velocity is independent of microtubule length (Hunt et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hunt et al., 1994.

claim: In the PRC1-Kif4A system, the initial sliding velocity depends on the initial overlap length, but does not change as overlap length reduces during sliding.
source: Here, the initial sliding velocity depends on the initial overlap length, but in contrast to the Ase1p-Ncd or HSET systems, does not change as overlap length reduces during sliding (Figure 3(iii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3(iii) and is based on studies of the PRC1-Kif4A system.

claim: Both in vitro and in cells, microtubules display 'lattice defects', which are disruptions in the ordered arrangement of tubulin subunits in a polymer, extending over length scales ranging from 0.1 to 1 μm.
source: As a result, both in vitro and in cells, microtubules display 'lattice defects', which are disruptions in the ordered arrangement of tubulin subunits in a polymer, extending over length scales ranging from 0.1 to 1 μm (Chrétien et al., 1992; Atherton et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on lattice defects.

claim: A mismatch in protofilament number on the lattice can lead to an increase in catastrophe frequency.
source: For instance, a mismatch in protofilament number on the lattice can lead to an increase in catastrophe frequency (Rai et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rai et al., 2021.

claim: Studies in animal cells have shown that damage to microtubule lattices can result in an increase in the length and stability of microtubules.
source: Somewhat counterintuitively, studies in animal cells have shown that damage to microtubule lattices can result in an increase in the length and stability of microtubules (Aumeier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aumeier et al., 2016.

claim: Sites of damage in the middle of a microtubule can incorporate GTP-tubulin dimers, as observed in live cells and in microtubules polymerized in vitro.
source: Several lines of experimental evidence indicate that sites of damage in the middle of a microtubule can incorporate GTP-tubulin dimers, as observed in live cells (Dimitrov et al., 2008; de Forges et al., 2016) and in microtubules polymerized in vitro (Schaedel et al., 2015; Schaedel et al., 2019; Rai et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in cells and in vitro.

claim: GTP-islands promote microtubule growth by serving as rescue points for re-initiation of growth during subsequent catastrophe events.
source: These 'GTP-islands' promote microtubule growth in two ways: (i) by serving as rescue points for re-initiation of growth during subsequent catastrophe events (Dimitrov et al., 2008; Tropini et al., 2012; Aumeier et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on GTP-islands.

claim: GTP-islands promote microtubule growth through the recruitment of growth-promoting MAPs that specifically recognize and bind to GTP-tubulin over GDP-tubulin, such as CLIP-170 and CLASP.
source: and (ii) through the recruitment of growth-promoting MAPs that specifically recognize and bind to GTP-tubulin over GDP-tubulin, such as the rescue factors cytoplasmic linker protein of 170 kDa (CLIP-170) and CLIP-associating protein (CLASP) (Figure 4(i); Folker et al., 2005; de Forges et al., 2016; Aher et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on rescue factors and reference to Figure 4(i).

claim: Sites of damage can result in microtubules that have significantly longer lifetimes, lengths, and rescue frequencies compared to microtubules undergoing stochastic polymerization and depolymerization.
source: Consequently, as demonstrated by in vitro studies, sites of damage can result in microtubules that have significantly longer lifetimes, lengths, and rescue frequencies compared to microtubules undergoing stochastic polymerization and depolymerization (Aumeier et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to in vitro studies.

claim: Some severing enzymes like katanin have been predicted to preferentially bind to sites of lattice damage on microtubules, based on in vitro experiments and simulations.
source: Some severing enzymes like katanin have been predicted to preferentially bind to sites of lattice damage on microtubules, based on in vitro experiments and simulations (Davis et al., 2002; Díaz-Valencia et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vitro experiments and simulations.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans meiotic spindles, the severing of microtubules by katanin leads to a steep decrease in microtubule density near the poles and an increase in microtubule density at the cell center.
source: For example, in Caenorhabditis elegans meiotic spindles, the severing of microtubules by katanin leads to a steep decrease in microtubule density near the poles and an increase in microtubule density at the cell center (Srayko et al., 2006; McNally et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in C. elegans.

claim: The activity of katanin in C. elegans meiotic spindles was found to cause an increase in the overall cellular microtubule mass.
source: Curiously, instead of conserving the total microtubule mass, the activity of katanin in this system was found to cause an increase in the overall cellular microtubule mass.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the C. elegans studies mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: In vitro studies on the severing enzymes katanin and spastin have shown that the activity of severing enzymes leads to the removal of tubulin dimers and causes lattice damage.
source: In vitro studies on the severing enzymes katanin and spastin have provided an explanation, showing that the activity of severing enzymes leads to the removal of tubulin dimers and causes lattice damage (Vemu et al., 2018; Kuo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: Soluble tubulin can bind katanin and inhibit its activity, thus setting up a feedback loop for the control of microtubule length and density.
source: In vitro, it has also been shown that soluble tubulin itself can bind katanin and inhibit its activity, thus setting up a feedback loop for the control of microtubule length and density (Bailey et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bailey et al., 2015.

claim: Stimulation of plant cells by blue light results in a dramatic reorientation of their cortical microtubules by ~90°, to specify a new cell elongation axis.
source: Stimulation of plant cells by blue light results in a dramatic reorientation of their cortical microtubules by ~90°, to specify a new cell elongation axis (Zandomeni and Schopfer, 1993; Paredez et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on plant cortical array reorientation.

claim: The microtubules of the longitudinal array play a critical role in directing array reorientation in plant cells.
source: The microtubules of the longitudinal array play a critical role in directing array reorientation (Lindeboom et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lindeboom et al., 2013.

claim: The process of plant cortical array reorientation begins with γ-TuRC-mediated branching microtubule nucleation, from the microtubules in the longitudinal array.
source: The process begins with γ-TuRC-mediated branching microtubule nucleation, from the microtubules in the longitudinal array.
evidence: This claim describes a mechanism based on the studies cited in the section.

claim: Branching nucleation from the longitudinal array results in new microtubules which grow at angles close to ±40° to the longitudinal array.
source: This results in new microtubules which grow at angles close to ±40° (hereafter referred to as diagonal microtubules) to the longitudinal array.
evidence: This claim describes a mechanism based on the studies cited in the section.

claim: The severing enzyme katanin is specifically recruited to sites where two microtubules cross over during plant cortical array reorientation.
source: For this, the severing enzyme katanin is specifically recruited to sites where two microtubules cross over (Zhang et al., 2013; Deinum et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on katanin recruitment.

claim: At cross-over sites, the frequency of katanin severing is higher on the new microtubule compared to microtubules of the original array.
source: At these sites, the frequency of katanin severing is higher on the new microtubule compared to microtubules of the original array, although the precise mechanism for selective severing is currently unknown.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the studies cited in the section.

claim: Katanin severing of a new microtubule generates two microtubules, doubling the number of transverse and diagonal microtubules that continue to grow.
source: Katanin severing of a new microtubule generates two microtubules, doubling the number of transverse and diagonal microtubules that continue to grow (Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2018.

claim: A new microtubule forms the maximum number of cross-overs when it grows perpendicular to the original array, compared to all other orientations.
source: Basic geometry dictates that this condition is satisfied when the new microtubule grows perpendicular to the original array, compared to all other orientations, thereby selectively amplifying the transverse microtubules.
evidence: This claim is based on geometric reasoning.

claim: The spindle midzone is an inter-digitating array of anti-parallel microtubules at the cell center.
source: The spindle midzone is an inter-digitating array of anti-parallel microtubules at the cell center. (Mastronarde et al., 1993; Figure 5(ii)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mastronarde et al., 1993 and reference to Figure 5(ii).

claim: The precise cellular location and size of the spindle midzone determine the site of cell cleavage during cytokinesis and ensure error-free genome propagation.
source: The precise cellular location and size of the spindle midzone determine the site of cell cleavage during cytokinesis and ensure error-free genome propagation (Eggert et al., 2006; Scholey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on spindle midzone function.

claim: Microtubules growing radially outward from the centrosomes serve as platforms for γ-TuRC and augmin-mediated branching nucleation resulting in new microtubules that grow with their plus-ends oriented toward the cell center.
source: For this, microtubules growing radially outward from the centrosomes serve as platforms for γ-TuRC and augmin-mediated branching nucleation resulting in new microtubules that grow with their plus-ends oriented toward the cell center (Uehara and Goshima, 2010; Uehara et al., 2016; Pamula et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on spindle midzone assembly.

claim: Length-dependent depolymerization ensures that microtubules have uniform length, and overlaps between anti-parallel microtubules are formed at the center of the cell.
source: Length-dependent depolymerization ensures that microtubules have uniform length, and overlaps between anti-parallel microtubules are formed at the center of the cell (Varga et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2009; Rizk et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on length-dependent depolymerization.

claim: Microtubule overlap length regulates microtubule polymerization dynamics and relative sliding of microtubules by several midzone kinesins including kinesin-5, kinesin-6, kinesin-14, and the Kif4A-PRC1 complex.
source: This is because microtubule overlap length regulates microtubule polymerization dynamics and relative sliding of microtubules by several midzone kinesins. These include kinesin-5, kinesin-6, kinesin-14,, and the Kif4A-PRC1 complex (Glotzer, 2009; Bieling et al., 2010; Subramanian and Kapoor, 2012; Scholey et al., 2016; Wijeratne and Subramanian, 2018; Shimamoto et al., 2015; Hannabuss et al., 2019; Krüger et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on midzone kinesins.

claim: As sliding progresses, overlap length-dependent braking forces generated by motor and non-motor MAPs increase, while the rate of sliding decreases, to establish a stable midzone of defined length.
source: As sliding progresses, overlap length-dependent braking forces generated by motor and non-motor MAPs increase, while the rate of sliding decreases, to establish a stable midzone of defined length (Braun et al., 2011; Braun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on braking forces.

claim: Microtubules have been shown to regulate the nucleation, polymerization, and dynamics of the actin network in migrating cells, neuronal growth cones, and dendritic spines.
source: For example, microtubules have been shown to regulate the nucleation, polymerization, and dynamics of the actin network in migrating cells, neuronal growth cones, and dendritic spines.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of cytoskeletal crosstalk.
